Chandrika

passage:
I'm Indu, Ganga's roommate. The week before her campus placement interview, she practised with me every night.
Ganga finds eye contact hard. She's always been like that; when she talks, she looks at your shoulder or the wall. But she listens better than anyone I know. She remembers everything.
Her senior told her, "Look the interviewer in the eye the whole time. It shows confidence." So she tried. She stared at me, unblinking, for five minutes. It was so intense I started laughing.
We tried something softer: look at the eyes when starting an answer and when finishing, and at the nose or eyebrows in between. Take breaks to look at notes.
On the day, she came back smiling. "I looked at them enough. And I looked at my notes when I was thinking."
She got the offer. The panel wrote she was "attentive and thoughtful."

qa.q: What did Ganga's senior tell her to do?
qa.a: Look the interviewer in the eye the whole time.

qa.q: What was Ganga probably feeling about the eye-contact advice?
qa.a: Ganga was likely anxious and uncomfortable, since eye contact is hard for her, and she overdid it when trying to follow the senior's advice.

qa.q: What approach worked for Ganga?
qa.a: A softer pattern of eye contact at the start and end of answers, with breaks to look at notes, which showed confidence without strain.

qa.q: How did the interview panel see Ganga?
qa.a: They saw her as attentive and thoughtful, even though she used less eye contact than her senior advised.

grounding: A roommate's account shows a young adult adjusting gaze for an interview, and that someone who finds eye contact hard can still listen well.

passage:
Jahnavi, you're worried because you can't hold eye contact in your interview? Let me, your Binita Masi, tell you about my first job interview.
I was twenty-one. Terribly shy. Couldn't look anyone in the eye for more than a second. My friends said, "You'll fail. Interviewers think you're hiding something."
In the room, I looked at the table, the window, my hands. But I listened to every word. When the panel asked me a long question about the accounts, I answered every part of it, in order.
At the end, the senior manager said, "You don't look at people much, do you?" I went cold. Then he said, "But you're the only candidate who answered the whole question."
I got the job. Years later, he told me, "Eye contact is nice. Listening is better."
So practise a little. Look up when you start and finish. But don't let anyone tell you that looking away means you're not listening.

qa.q: How old was Binita at her first job interview?
qa.a: Twenty-one.

qa.q: How did Binita feel in her first interview?
qa.a: She felt painfully shy and nervous, unable to hold eye contact, and went cold when the manager noticed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Binita Masi's story?
qa.a: The manager noticing that she was the only candidate who answered the whole question, showing that listening mattered more than eye contact.

qa.q: How did the senior manager see Binita's lack of eye contact?
qa.a: He noticed it but valued her careful listening more, later saying listening is better than eye contact.

grounding: The elder's story shows a shy young adult who found eye contact hard but listened well, and adjusting gaze a little for interviews.

passage: Pankaj had spent a month training for job interviews: firm handshake, steady eye contact, no looking at the floor. It worked; he got the offer. So on Saturday, meeting Aparna for coffee after their families had exchanged numbers, he did the same. The café near the station was deafening, a blender roaring every two minutes, and Aparna had exactly half an hour before her train. Pankaj leaned in and held her gaze, unblinking, while she talked about her botany course. Aparna's sentences got shorter. She kept looking at the sugar packets. "Is something wrong?" she finally asked. "You're looking at me like an exam invigilator." Pankaj laughed, embarrassed, and let his eyes drift to the window and back. "Sorry. Interview habits." Aparna relaxed. "I'm the opposite. I look everywhere except faces, especially when I'm nervous. But I'm listening, promise. You said your sister also studies botany?" She had heard every word.

qa.a: Aparna had exactly half an hour before her train.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when Aparna mentioned an exam invigilator?
qa.a: Pankaj felt embarrassed, laughing awkwardly, realising the interview habit didn't fit a coffee date.

qa.q: How did Pankaj adjust, and why did it help?
qa.a: He let his gaze drift to the window and back, softening it for a date instead of an interview, which let Aparna relax.

qa.q: What was the stare like for Aparna?
qa.a: Aparna felt uncomfortable, her sentences shrinking and eyes on the sugar packets; she finds eye contact hard herself but was still listening closely.
